dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: What is the default page (block) size used by PostgreSQL for table and index files?
options: 4 KB
8 KB
16 KB
64 KB
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: PostgreSQL uses 8 KB blocks by default (a compile-time setting). 16 KB is the default page size of MySQL InnoDB, which is the most common mix-up.

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: Why do database engines read and write data in fixed-size pages rather than fetching individual rows from disk?
options: Rows cannot be located on disk without first loading the full page directory into memory
Storage I/O is block-oriented, so fetching one row costs a whole block anyway; pages make caching and I/O uniform
Fixed-size pages let the engine skip writing a write-ahead log for most changes
SQL requires every row to be padded to the page size for alignment
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: Disks and the OS transfer whole blocks, so reading one row already pays for its block. Pages give the buffer pool a uniform unit to cache, evict and write. Pages don't remove the need for WAL; logging is separate.

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: A table is stored as a heap file and has no indexes. A query asks for the row with id = 42. What must the engine do?
options: Binary-search the heap, because rows are kept sorted by insertion id
Jump to the page computed from id modulo the number of pages
Scan pages sequentially, because heap rows have no guaranteed order
Read only the last page, where the newest rows are always kept
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: A heap file places rows wherever free space exists, so there is no ordering to exploit; without an index the only option is a sequential scan. Binary search would need the heap to be sorted, which it isn't.

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: Why do engines like PostgreSQL and InnoDB avoid using plain LRU for buffer pool eviction?
options: LRU needs a timestamp on every page, which would exceed the page header size
LRU cannot evict dirty pages, so the pool would fill with modified data
LRU only works when every page in the pool has the same access frequency
One large sequential scan would push out the hot working set (sequential flooding)
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: Under pure LRU, scanning a huge table once makes every scanned page 'most recent' and flushes the frequently used pages. PostgreSQL uses clock-sweep plus small ring buffers for big scans; InnoDB inserts new pages at a midpoint of its LRU list. LRU can evict dirty pages; they just need writing first.

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL with synchronous_commit = on, what must be durably on disk before COMMIT returns to the client?
options: Every modified data page of the transaction, written to its table file
The WAL records up to and including the transaction's commit record
A full checkpoint covering all dirty pages in shared buffers
Both the WAL and every index page touched by the transaction
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: Commit forces the WAL to disk; the modified data pages may stay dirty in shared buffers and are written later by the background writer or checkpointer (no-force policy). After a crash, replaying the WAL rebuilds them. Forcing data pages at commit would make every commit pay for random writes.

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: Many engines use a slotted-page layout with a slot directory at the start of each page. What problem does the slot directory solve?
options: Rows can move within the page during compaction without changing their external (page, slot) identifier
It lets each row span multiple pages without needing overflow storage
It stores a checksum per row so torn writes can be detected
It keeps rows physically sorted by primary key inside the page
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: Indexes reference a row by (page, slot), e.g. PostgreSQL's ctid. The slot holds the row's offset, so the engine can compact free space and move bytes around while the identifier stays valid. It doesn't sort rows or handle multi-page rows (PostgreSQL uses TOAST for that).

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: What does it mean when a page in the buffer pool is 'pinned'?
options: It has been modified and is waiting to be flushed to disk
It was marked by the DBA to stay in memory permanently
An active operation is using it, so it cannot be evicted right now
It belongs to a system catalog and is never written back
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: A pin count tracks how many operations are currently using a buffer. While it is non-zero the page can't be evicted. 'Modified but not flushed' describes a dirty page, which is a separate flag.

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: Which statements about the buffer pool are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A dirty page is one modified in memory but not yet written to its data file
Evicting a dirty page requires writing it out first
A pinned page may be evicted as long as it is clean
The buffer pool caches individual rows rather than whole pages
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: Dirty means changed in memory only, so it must be written before its frame is reused. Pinned pages can't be evicted whether clean or dirty, and the buffer pool's unit of caching is the page, not the row.

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: Why can a full sequential scan of a heap be cheaper per row than fetching the same rows through random index lookups? Select all that apply.
options: Sequential reads allow the OS and storage to prefetch ahead
Each page read during the scan yields many rows
Random lookups may need a different page for nearly every row
Heap files keep rows sorted by primary key, so the scan can stop early
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: Sequential I/O benefits from read-ahead and amortises each page over many rows, while index-driven fetches may touch one page per row. Heaps are unordered, so a sequential scan cannot stop early on a key.

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE writes a new version of the row (tuple) instead of overwriting the old version in place.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: PostgreSQL's MVCC keeps the old tuple for transactions that still need it and writes a new tuple; VACUUM reclaims dead versions later. InnoDB updates in place and keeps old versions in undo logs instead.

dbms-storage-indexing:0.prompt: Doubling the buffer pool size always halves disk reads, because every page access then hits memory.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:0.explanation: Hit rate depends on the working set and access pattern. If the hot set already fits, extra memory changes little; if the data is far larger than memory or accessed uniformly, misses fall less than proportionally.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: What is the key structural difference between a B+ tree and a classic B-tree?
options: A B+ tree allows only two children per node, while a B-tree allows many
A B+ tree stores records in every node, while a B-tree stores them only in leaves
A B+ tree is unbalanced to favour recent keys, while a B-tree is always balanced
A B+ tree keeps records only in leaves, which are linked; internal nodes hold routing keys
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: In a B+ tree, internal nodes contain only separator keys and child pointers, and all data (or row pointers) lives in leaves chained in key order. A classic B-tree stores records in internal nodes too. Both are balanced and high-fanout.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: Why are B+ trees well suited to range queries such as WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 20?
options: Every internal node stores the minimum and maximum of its subtree's rows
After descending to the first matching leaf, the scan follows leaf links in key order
The tree is rebuilt in sorted order whenever a range query arrives
Range queries are answered from the root node without visiting leaves
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: One root-to-leaf descent finds the start of the range; sibling links then let the engine read leaves sequentially until the end. Without leaf links it would have to go back up the tree for the next key.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: Why does keeping only keys in the internal nodes of a B+ tree reduce I/O compared with a B-tree that stores full records in every node?
options: More keys fit per page, so fanout is higher and the tree is shallower
Internal nodes no longer need to be written to disk at all
Keys are compressed into hashes, which makes comparisons faster
Leaves can then be skipped during point lookups
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: Without record payloads, an internal page holds hundreds of keys, which raises fanout and lowers height, so a lookup reads fewer pages. Internal nodes are still persisted, and point lookups still end at a leaf.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: A B+ tree index has a fanout of about 500 per node. Roughly how many levels are needed to index 1 billion keys?
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: 500^3 = 125 million, which is less than 1 billion; 500^4 = 62.5 billion, which is enough. So about 4 levels. In practice the top levels are cached, so a lookup costs one or two disk reads. 9 would be closer to a binary tree's growth rate.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: A MySQL InnoDB table uses random UUIDv4 values as its primary key and inserts slow down as the table grows. What is the most likely cause?
options: UUID comparisons are much slower than integer comparisons
InnoDB rebuilds the whole clustered index after each insert with a non-integer key
Inserts land on random leaves, causing page splits, half-full pages and poor cache locality
UUIDv4 values collide often, so InnoDB retries inserts frequently
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: The clustered B+ tree is ordered by the key, so random keys hit random leaves; once the index exceeds memory, each insert may need a disk read and frequent splits. Time-ordered keys (auto-increment, UUIDv7) append to the rightmost leaf. Comparison cost is minor in comparison.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: When does the height of a B+ tree increase?
options: Whenever any leaf node splits
Only when the root node splits
When the number of keys exceeds the fanout
When a rotation is needed to rebalance a subtree
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: A full node splits and pushes a separator into its parent; splits can cascade upward. Height grows only when the root itself splits and a new root is created, which is why all leaves stay at the same depth. Rotations belong to binary trees like AVL, not B+ trees.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: Which is an advantage a classic B-tree has over a B+ tree?
options: Range scans are faster because leaves are linked in both directions
Internal nodes have higher fanout because they store records
A point lookup can finish at an internal node if the key is stored there
It never needs to split nodes on insert
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: Because a B-tree stores records in internal nodes too, some lookups end before reaching a leaf. The cost is lower fanout (records take space) and no leaf chain for range scans, which is why databases favour B+ trees.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: Which statements about B+ trees used as database indexes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Every root-to-leaf path has the same length
Lookups, inserts and deletes take O(log n) page accesses
In the textbook algorithm, non-root nodes are kept at least half full
Each node has exactly two children, like a binary search tree
A range scan must return to the root to find each next key
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: B+ trees are balanced, high-fanout trees with logarithmic operations and a minimum occupancy rule. They are not binary, and leaf links make range scans sequential without going back to the root.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: A table has a B+ tree index on column k. Which queries benefit from the linked leaf level? Select all that apply.
options: SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY k LIMIT 10
SELECT * FROM t WHERE k BETWEEN 100 AND 200
SELECT * FROM t WHERE k = 42, where k is unique
SELECT count(DISTINCT other_col) FROM t, where other_col is unindexed
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: Ordered retrieval and range predicates walk leaves in key order. A unique equality lookup is a single descent that doesn't follow sibling links, and a query on an unindexed column can't use the index at all.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: A B+ tree stays balanced: every path from the root to a leaf has the same length.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: Splits propagate upward and the tree grows only at the root, so all leaves are always at the same depth. That gives predictable lookup cost.

dbms-storage-indexing:1.prompt: On disk, a balanced binary search tree such as a red-black tree is about as efficient as a B+ tree, since both have O(log n) lookups.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:1.explanation: Both are O(log n), but the base differs. A binary tree needs about log2(n) node visits (around 30 for a billion keys), each potentially a page read, while a B+ tree with fanout in the hundreds needs only 3 to 4. On disk, the constant factor is what matters.

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: In MySQL InnoDB, what is the clustered index of a table?
options: Whichever index was created first on the table
The primary key B+ tree, whose leaves store the full rows
A separate copy of the table sorted by the most queried column
An optional index created with CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: InnoDB stores the table itself as a B+ tree keyed by the primary key, with rows in the leaves. It isn't chosen by creation order, and MySQL has no CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX syntax (that's SQL Server).

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: Why can a table have at most one clustered index?
options: The SQL standard limits each table to one index of each type
Rows can be physically stored in only one order
Clustered indexes use too much memory to have more than one
A second clustered index would break foreign key constraints
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: A clustered index decides the physical order of the rows themselves, and data can only be laid out one way. Secondary indexes store keys plus a pointer, so there can be many of them.

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: In MySQL InnoDB, what does a leaf entry of a secondary index store to locate the full row?
options: The physical page number and slot of the row
A hash of the row's contents
The row's primary key value
A copy of every column in the row
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: InnoDB secondary indexes store the primary key, so a lookup traverses the secondary index and then the clustered index. This keeps secondary indexes valid when rows move during page splits. PostgreSQL, by contrast, stores a physical TID.

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: Why does a wide primary key (for example a composite of two long VARCHARs) hurt an InnoDB table with several secondary indexes?
options: InnoDB cannot build secondary indexes on tables with composite keys
Wide primary keys turn off the adaptive hash index
Each secondary index entry repeats the primary key, so all those indexes grow
The clustered index is rebuilt every time a secondary index is read
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: Every secondary index leaf carries the full primary key as its row pointer, so a wide PK enlarges every index, reduces fanout and wastes buffer pool space. A compact surrogate key avoids this.

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a team runs CLUSTER orders USING orders_created_at_idx. What happens to rows inserted afterwards?
options: They are placed wherever there is free space; the physical order is not maintained
They are automatically inserted in created_at order, as in InnoDB
Inserts fail until the table is unclustered
They go to a separate overflow heap that is merged at the next VACUUM
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: PostgreSQL tables are always heaps. CLUSTER rewrites the table once in index order, but later inserts and updates aren't kept in order, so you would need to run CLUSTER again (which takes an exclusive lock). PostgreSQL has no continuously maintained clustered index like InnoDB.

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: In PostgreSQL, why can an UPDATE that changes only a non-indexed column often avoid touching any index?
options: PostgreSQL updates rows in place, so index pointers stay valid
Index entries point to the primary key, which didn't change
Indexes are updated lazily by VACUUM rather than by the UPDATE
A HOT update puts the new version on the same page, chained from the old one
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: A heap-only tuple (HOT) update is possible when no indexed column changes and the page has free space. The existing index entries reach the new version via the chain on that page. PostgreSQL doesn't update in place, and its indexes point to TIDs, not primary keys.

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: A query returns 200,000 rows by a date range. Why is a range scan on the clustered key usually much cheaper than using a non-covering secondary index on that date?
options: Secondary indexes cannot answer range predicates
On the clustered key the rows are contiguous; through a secondary index each row may need a separate random fetch
Clustered indexes are always kept fully in memory
The optimizer adds a sort step to every secondary index scan
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: Clustered order means matching rows sit together on consecutive pages. A non-covering secondary index gives keys in order, but the rows are scattered, so each one may cost a random lookup. Secondary B-tree indexes do support ranges.

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: Which statements about MySQL InnoDB indexes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: If no primary key is defined, InnoDB clusters on the first UNIQUE index whose columns are all NOT NULL, or else a hidden row ID
A secondary index lookup that needs non-indexed columns also searches the clustered index
Secondary indexes store the physical page address of each row
Changing a row's primary key value only needs a change to the clustered index
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: InnoDB always has a clustered index, falling back to a suitable unique index or a hidden 6-byte row ID. Secondary lookups go through the PK. Because secondary entries contain the PK, changing it also means updating every secondary index (and moving the row).

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: Which primary key choices keep inserts into an InnoDB clustered index mostly append-only at the right edge of the tree? Select all that apply.
options: BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT
UUIDv7 stored as BINARY(16)
Random UUIDv4 stored as BINARY(16)
A SHA-256 hash of the user's email
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: Auto-increment and UUIDv7 (time-ordered prefix) both grow over time, so new rows land on the rightmost leaf. UUIDv4 and hashes are uniformly random, so they scatter inserts across the tree and cause splits.

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: In PostgreSQL, the primary key index is a clustered index that keeps table rows physically ordered by the key.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: In PostgreSQL every index, including the primary key, is secondary and points into an unordered heap. Only InnoDB-style engines (and SQL Server's clustered indexes) store rows in key order.

dbms-storage-indexing:2.prompt: In an InnoDB table, a query that reads only a secondary index's columns plus primary key columns can be answered from the secondary index alone.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:2.explanation: Secondary index leaves already contain the primary key, so those columns are 'covered' without a trip to the clustered index. EXPLAIN shows this as 'Using index'.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: A table has a B-tree index on (last_name, first_name). Which query cannot seek into the index efficiently, assuming no skip-scan?
options: WHERE last_name = 'Rao'
WHERE last_name = 'Rao' AND first_name = 'Ana'
WHERE first_name = 'Ana'
WHERE last_name LIKE 'Ra%' with a C-collation column
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: Entries are sorted by last_name first, so the first_name values for 'Ana' are scattered across the whole index. A leading-column equality or prefix match can seek; a condition on only the second column cannot.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: What makes an index 'covering' for a particular query?
options: It contains every column the query needs, so the table rows don't have to be read
It covers every row in the table, unlike a partial index
It is the only index on the table, so the planner has to choose it
It includes every column of the table in its key
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: Covering is relative to a query: if all referenced columns are in the index, the engine can do an index-only scan. It doesn't need every table column, and a partial index can still cover queries that match its predicate.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: Index: (status, created_at). Query: WHERE status = 'open' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. What can a B-tree engine do?
options: Use the index for status only, then sort all open rows by created_at
Ignore the index because DESC order needs a descending index
Seek to status = 'open' and read created_at in reverse order, stopping after 20 rows
Use the index only if created_at is also listed first
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: With equality on the leading column, the matching entries are already ordered by created_at, and B-trees can be scanned backwards. So the LIMIT stops after 20 entries with no sort. A separate DESC index isn't needed for a single-column direction.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: With a B-tree index on (a, b), how is the predicate WHERE a > 10 AND b = 5 typically handled?
options: Both columns are used to seek, jumping directly to each (a, 5)
The index can't be used because the range comes first
The engine seeks on b = 5 first, then filters on a
The engine seeks on a > 10, and b = 5 is checked as a filter while scanning that range
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: After a range on the leading column, the b values aren't ordered across the whole range, so b can only be checked entry by entry. This is why equality columns should come before range columns in a composite index. (Some engines add skip scans, but that isn't a standard seek.)

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: A multi-tenant API mostly runs WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND created_at >= $2. Which composite index is the better choice?
options: (created_at, tenant_id), because the range is the most selective part
(tenant_id, created_at), with the equality column first and the range last
Two separate single-column indexes, which will always be combined
(tenant_id) alone, because created_at changes too often to index
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: Equality-first ordering lets the engine seek to one tenant and then scan a contiguous created_at range. With created_at first, the scan covers every tenant in the time range and has to filter on tenant_id. Combining two indexes (bitmap AND) is usually slower than one well-ordered composite.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what is the purpose of CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total)?
options: Make total part of the sort key so ORDER BY total uses the index
Enforce that total is unique per customer
Store total in the leaf entries so queries on customer_id that read total can use index-only scans
Create a second index on total that is maintained together with the first
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: INCLUDE columns are non-key payload stored only in the leaves. They support index-only scans without affecting ordering or uniqueness, and they don't bloat the upper levels of the tree. They aren't searchable or sortable as keys.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 'Index Only Scan ... Heap Fetches: 48000' for a query fully covered by the index. What is the most likely cause?
options: Many pages aren't marked all-visible in the visibility map, so the heap must be checked; VACUUM fixes it
The index is corrupted and PostgreSQL is falling back to the heap
INCLUDE columns are always read from the heap
Index-only scans always read the heap in PostgreSQL, so the counter is just informational
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: Index entries carry no visibility information. PostgreSQL can skip the heap only for pages that the visibility map marks all-visible, which VACUUM sets. On a recently modified table many pages aren't marked, so the scan fetches heap tuples.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: With a B-tree index on (a, b, c) and no WHERE clause, which ORDER BY clauses can be satisfied by reading the index in order, without a sort? Select all that apply.
options: ORDER BY a
ORDER BY a, b
ORDER BY b, c
ORDER BY a, c
ORDER BY a DESC, b DESC
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: Any leading prefix in the index order works, and the whole index can be read backwards for uniformly reversed directions. ORDER BY b, c skips the leading column, and ORDER BY a, c skips b, so neither matches the index order.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: A table has B-tree indexes on (a) and on (a, b). Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: (a, b) can serve WHERE a = ? lookups, so (a) is usually redundant
Dropping (a) reduces the work done on every insert
(a, b) can seek directly on WHERE b = ?
(a) must exist for the planner to use (a, b)
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: A composite index serves its leading-column predicates, so a separate (a) mostly duplicates it while costing write and memory overhead. (a, b) can't seek on b alone, and composite indexes don't depend on single-column indexes.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: With a B-tree index on (a, b), the query WHERE b = 3 AND a = 7 can use the index on both columns even though b is written first in the WHERE clause.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: The order of predicates in WHERE doesn't matter; the optimizer matches conditions to index columns. What matters is that the leading column a has a usable condition.

dbms-storage-indexing:3.prompt: Adding extra columns to a covering index has no downside, because indexes are only read and never written.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:3.explanation: Every insert, and every update of an included column, has to maintain the index. Wider entries also mean a bigger index, lower fanout and more buffer pool pressure. Covering indexes trade write cost and space for read speed.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: Which predicate can a hash index on column email help with?
options: email > 'm'
email = 'a@example.com'
email LIKE 'admin%'
ORDER BY email
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: A hash index maps each value to a bucket through a hash function, so it only supports equality. Ranges, prefix matches and ordering need a sorted structure like a B-tree.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: Why can't a hash index be used to return rows in ORDER BY order?
options: Hash indexes store only NULL-free columns
Hash buckets are kept in insertion order, not key order
Hashing scatters neighbouring keys, so the index has no key order to follow
Hash indexes are rebuilt on every query
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: A good hash function deliberately spreads similar keys across buckets, so the structure keeps no ordering. Buckets aren't kept in insertion order either; the key order is simply lost.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, which statement about hash indexes is accurate?
options: They are WAL-logged (since version 10) but support only = and cannot back a UNIQUE constraint
They are not crash-safe and must be rebuilt after a crash
They are the default index type for text columns
They support range scans once the table has been ANALYZEd
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: Before PostgreSQL 10, hash indexes weren't WAL-logged, which is why old advice says to avoid them. Today they are crash-safe and replicated, but only B-tree supports uniqueness, and hash still handles only equality. B-tree is the default type.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, when might a hash index be a better choice than a B-tree for equality lookups?
options: When the column has very few distinct values
When queries also need ORDER BY on the column
When the indexed values are long, such as full URLs, since hash entries store a fixed 4-byte hash code
When the table is mostly written and rarely read
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: A PostgreSQL hash index stores only the 32-bit hash per entry, so it can be much smaller than a B-tree holding the long keys themselves. Low cardinality causes long bucket chains, and ORDER BY needs a B-tree.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: Why do on-disk hash indexes use schemes like extendible or linear hashing instead of rehashing everything when the buckets fill?
options: They keep keys sorted inside each bucket
They grow by splitting one bucket at a time, avoiding a huge one-off rehash
They remove the need for overflow pages entirely in every case
They allow the hash function to change for each query
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: A full rehash of a large on-disk index would stall writes for a long time. Extendible and linear hashing split buckets incrementally as the index grows. They reduce overflow chains but don't sort keys or remove overflow entirely.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: A hash index is built on a column where 40% of rows share the same value. What happens to lookups for that value?
options: They stay O(1), because the hash function spreads duplicates evenly
The index automatically switches to a B-tree for that value
The duplicates are stored once with a count, so lookups are faster
They hit one bucket with a long overflow chain, so the lookup degrades badly
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: Identical values always hash to the same bucket, so heavy skew piles up entries in one bucket and its overflow pages. Hash indexes suit high-cardinality columns; for such a common value a sequential scan is usually better anyway.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: In MySQL InnoDB, what is the adaptive hash index?
options: An in-memory hash that InnoDB builds automatically over frequently accessed B-tree index pages
A persistent hash index created with CREATE INDEX ... USING HASH
A hash of each row used to detect replication drift
A hash partitioning scheme for very large tables
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: InnoDB watches index lookups and, for hot pages, builds an in-memory hash to skip B-tree descents. It is controlled by innodb_adaptive_hash_index, not by DDL. InnoDB doesn't support persistent hash indexes; USING HASH falls back to a B-tree.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: Which are limitations of PostgreSQL hash indexes compared with B-tree indexes? Select all that apply.
options: No support for range predicates like < or BETWEEN
Cannot be used to satisfy ORDER BY
Cannot be built on more than one column
Cannot be used for equality lookups
Always larger on disk than an equivalent B-tree
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: PostgreSQL hash indexes are single-column, equality-only and unordered. Equality is exactly what they do support, and they are often smaller than a B-tree on wide keys because they store only hash codes.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: Which access patterns suit a hash-based index well? Select all that apply.
options: Looking up a session by its exact random token
A key-value store fetching values by exact key
Finding orders placed in the last 7 days
Returning the top 10 players by score
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: Exact-match lookups on high-cardinality keys are ideal for hashing. Time ranges and top-N by score need ordered access, which a B-tree (or a sorted structure such as a Redis sorted set) provides.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: A hash index lookup is O(1) on average, but a range predicate like price BETWEEN 10 AND 20 still requires a table scan or a different index.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: Hashing gives constant expected time for equality but keeps no ordering, so it can't enumerate a range. A B-tree on price would serve the range.

dbms-storage-indexing:4.prompt: In MySQL InnoDB, CREATE INDEX idx ON t (col) USING HASH creates a persistent on-disk hash index.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:4.explanation: InnoDB supports only B-tree (plus full-text and spatial) indexes. A USING HASH clause is accepted but a B-tree is built. Hash indexes are available in the MEMORY engine, and InnoDB's adaptive hash index is internal and in-memory.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: What makes an LSM tree write-optimised compared with an in-place B-tree?
options: It skips durability by keeping all writes only in memory
Writes are buffered in memory and flushed as sorted files sequentially, never updating pages in place
It stores data unsorted, so inserts never need comparisons
It writes each key to exactly one fixed disk location chosen by hashing
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: An LSM tree turns random writes into sequential ones: append to a WAL, insert into a memtable, then flush whole sorted SSTables. It stays durable through the WAL and keeps data sorted within each SSTable.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: In an LSM-tree storage engine, what does compaction do?
options: Compresses the memtable before it is written to the WAL
Merges SSTables, keeping the newest version of each key and dropping overwritten or deleted entries
Rebuilds the bloom filters without touching the data files
Sorts the write-ahead log so it can be replayed faster
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: Compaction merges sorted runs into new SSTables, discarding stale versions and expired tombstones. That bounds read cost and reclaims space. It works on SSTables, not the WAL or memtable.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: Why do LSM-based engines such as RocksDB and Cassandra keep a bloom filter per SSTable?
options: To store the key ranges of each SSTable in sorted order
To compress values so more fit in the block cache
To guarantee that every positive answer means the key is present
To skip SSTables that definitely don't contain a key, avoiding wasted reads on point lookups
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: A point read may otherwise have to check many SSTables. A bloom filter can say 'definitely not here' with no false negatives, so most irrelevant files are skipped. It can give false positives, so a 'maybe' still needs a read.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: How is a DELETE typically implemented in an LSM tree?
options: The key is removed from every SSTable that contains it immediately
A tombstone marker is written; the old data is physically removed during later compaction
The SSTable containing the key is deleted and rebuilt from the WAL
The key is moved to a separate deleted-keys SSTable that is never compacted
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: SSTables are immutable, so a delete is a new write: a tombstone that shadows older versions. Compaction eventually drops both. Editing existing SSTables in place would defeat the design.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: Which trade-off correctly compares leveled compaction with size-tiered compaction?
options: Leveled gives lower read and space amplification but higher write amplification
Leveled gives lower write amplification but higher read amplification
Size-tiered gives lower space amplification and lower read amplification
Both have the same amplification; they only differ in file naming
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: Leveled compaction keeps non-overlapping files per level, so reads check few files and little stale data remains, but data is rewritten many times. Size-tiered merges similar-sized runs less often, which lowers write amplification at the cost of more overlapping files and temporary space.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: A Cassandra table receives many deletes, and range reads over that partition then become very slow. What is the most likely cause?
options: Deleted rows are kept in the memtable forever
Bloom filters stop working after deletes
Range reads must skip over many tombstones that haven't yet been purged by compaction
Cassandra rebuilds the partition index on every delete
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: Tombstones remain until compaction runs after gc_grace_seconds, and reads must process them to know data is deleted. Heavy delete patterns (for example queue-like tables) cause tombstone-heavy reads. Bloom filters help point lookups, not range scans.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: Which of these storage engines is based on an LSM tree?
options: MySQL InnoDB
RocksDB
SQLite's default engine
PostgreSQL's heap with B-tree indexes
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: RocksDB (like LevelDB and Cassandra's storage) is an LSM engine. InnoDB and SQLite use B+ trees, and PostgreSQL uses heap files with B-tree indexes.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: Which statements about amplification in LSM trees are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Write amplification: the same data is rewritten several times as compaction moves it through levels
Read amplification: a point read may have to check several SSTables
Space amplification: obsolete versions use disk until compaction removes them
A well-tuned LSM tree eliminates all three kinds of amplification at once
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: LSM tuning is a trade-off between write, read and space amplification. Reducing one usually increases another (the RUM trade-off), so no setting removes all three.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: For which situations does an LSM tree usually have an advantage over a B-tree? Select all that apply.
options: High-volume ingestion such as metrics, logs or event streams
Better compression, because SSTables are immutable and sorted
The most predictable read latency, even while heavy compaction runs
Point reads that always touch exactly one page
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: Sequential writes and immutable sorted files favour ingestion throughput and compression. Compaction competes for I/O and can cause latency spikes, and point reads may check several levels, so predictable single-page reads are a B-tree strength.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: SSTables are mutable: updating a key rewrites that key's entry inside the existing SSTable file.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: SSTables are written once and never modified. An update is a new entry in the memtable that later lands in a newer SSTable; reads take the newest version, and compaction drops the old one.

dbms-storage-indexing:5.prompt: Because SSTables are sorted by key, compaction can merge them with a sequential, mergesort-style pass.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:5.explanation: Merging sorted runs needs only sequential reads of each input and a sequential write of the output, keeping the newest version of each key. That is why compaction is I/O-efficient even for large files.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: A table has 8 secondary indexes. Why are its INSERTs slower than on the same table with 1 index?
options: Each INSERT must also add an entry to every index, multiplying writes and WAL
The optimizer re-plans the INSERT once per index
Inserts are serialised behind a table lock whenever more than one index exists
Each index forces a full table scan to check for duplicates
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: Every index is another structure to update (and to log) for each new row. Non-unique indexes don't scan for duplicates, and inserts aren't serialised just because indexes exist.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: In PostgreSQL, 95% of rows have is_active = true. A query filters WHERE is_active = true, yet the planner ignores the index on is_active. Why?
options: Boolean columns can't be indexed in PostgreSQL
The index is too small to be considered
Fetching most of the table through the index costs more random I/O than a sequential scan
The planner never uses indexes for equality on booleans
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: With low selectivity, an index scan would visit nearly every page anyway, but in random order and with extra index reads. A sequential scan is cheaper, so the cost-based planner rightly picks it. Booleans can be indexed; it just isn't useful for the common value.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: You need to bulk-load 50 million rows into a new table that will have 6 secondary indexes. What is usually fastest?
options: Create all indexes first so each row is indexed as it arrives
Load the data first, then create the indexes, so each is built in one sorted pass
Load into a table with indexes, then REINDEX every index afterwards
Create the indexes with low fillfactor so inserts never split pages
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: Building an index from existing data sorts the keys once and writes compact pages, which is far cheaper than 50M individual inserts with random page splits. Creating indexes first and then reindexing pays the cost twice.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: In PostgreSQL, how can you find secondary indexes that are probably not being used?
options: Query pg_stat_user_indexes for indexes whose idx_scan stays at or near 0 over a representative period
Run EXPLAIN on a single SELECT and drop any index it doesn't use
Check pg_class for indexes larger than their table
Look for indexes created more than a year ago
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: idx_scan counts how often an index was used since stats were reset. One EXPLAIN only reflects one query; check over a full business cycle (including monthly jobs) and on replicas, and never drop indexes that back constraints.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a team adds an index on last_seen_at, which is updated on every request. Write I/O and table bloat jump. Why?
options: Timestamp indexes can't be vacuumed
Each update now changes an indexed column, so HOT updates are no longer possible and every index gets a new entry
PostgreSQL rewrites the whole table when an indexed column changes
The new index makes autovacuum skip the table
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: HOT updates require that no indexed column changes. Indexing a frequently updated column turns every update into a non-HOT update that inserts entries into all indexes, increasing WAL, bloat and vacuum work. The table isn't rewritten.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: A very high-concurrency insert workload uses a B-tree index on a monotonically increasing key. Under heavy load, inserts contend with each other. What is the likely cause?
options: Every insert targets the same rightmost leaf page, so they contend for its latch
Monotonic keys cause random page splits across the tree
The index degenerates into a linked list
The optimizer has to re-plan every insert
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: Sequential keys are good for locality, but at very high concurrency all writers hit the last leaf page, creating a hot spot (known as last-page insert contention). Random keys spread the load but cause the split and cache problems described for UUIDv4.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: A table has 15 indexes and its working set already exceeds RAM. Apart from write cost, how do the extra indexes hurt read queries?
options: Reads must check every index for consistency
The planner always merges all indexes, which slows every query
Index pages compete with hot data pages for buffer pool memory, increasing cache misses
Extra indexes force reads to take shared table locks
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: Indexes occupy cache too. Unused or redundant ones still get pulled in by writes and push useful pages out, so reads miss more often. Reads don't validate every index or merge them all.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: Which signs suggest a secondary index may not be worth keeping? Select all that apply.
options: Its idx_scan count has stayed near zero across a full business cycle
Its columns are a leading prefix of another existing index
It is used by a nightly report that would otherwise take hours
It backs a UNIQUE constraint the application relies on
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: An unused index or one made redundant by a wider composite index costs writes and memory for nothing. Rarely used indexes that save hours, or that enforce correctness (unique constraints), earn their cost.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: Which factors increase the cost of maintaining a secondary B-tree index? Select all that apply.
options: Randomly distributed keys that cause frequent page splits
Frequent updates to the indexed column
The table being a read-only archive
An append-only timestamp key written by a single writer
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: Random keys split pages all over the tree and hurt caching, and updating an indexed column means deleting and re-inserting index entries. A read-only table has no maintenance cost, and a single writer appending ordered keys is the cheap case.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: An index on a low-cardinality column can still help if queries filter on a rare value, such as status = 'failed' when only 0.1% of rows have failed.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: Selectivity depends on the value being searched, not just the number of distinct values. With accurate statistics the planner uses the index for rare values. A partial index WHERE status = 'failed' is even smaller.

dbms-storage-indexing:6.prompt: Because the optimizer simply ignores indexes it doesn't choose, an unused index has no cost.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:6.explanation: Every insert and relevant update must still maintain the index, it takes disk and buffer pool space, it adds WAL and vacuum work, and the planner has to consider it. Unused indexes are pure overhead.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: How is a bitmap index organised?
options: A B-tree whose leaves hold compressed row data
One bit vector per distinct value, with one bit per row showing whether the row has that value
A hash table mapping each row ID to its column values
A sorted list of row IDs per value, stored inside the table pages
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: For each distinct value there is a bitmap with bit i set when row i has that value. Combining predicates becomes bitwise operations. A sorted list of row IDs is a posting list, a related but different structure.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: Which workload suits a bitmap index best?
options: Read-mostly analytics filtering on low-cardinality columns like region or status
High-concurrency OLTP updating the indexed column on every request
Unique lookups by a primary key
Range scans on a high-cardinality timestamp
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: Bitmaps are compact and fast to combine when a column has few distinct values and data changes rarely, as in a data warehouse. Frequent updates cause contention, and unique or high-cardinality keys would need huge numbers of mostly empty bitmaps.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: A warehouse query filters WHERE gender = 'F' AND region = 'EU' AND status = 'active', and each column has a bitmap index. How is it evaluated efficiently?
options: By scanning the region index and filtering the other columns per row
By AND-ing the three bitmaps bit by bit, then fetching only rows whose bit is set
By joining the three indexes with a hash join
By sorting the table on all three columns first
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: A bitwise AND of the per-value bitmaps gives exactly the qualifying rows, using fast word-at-a-time CPU operations. This beats using one index and filtering the rest, especially when each predicate alone is unselective.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: Why are bitmap indexes a poor fit for OLTP tables with frequent concurrent updates to the indexed column?
options: Bitmaps can't represent NULL values
Changing a row's value updates compressed bitmap segments that cover many rows, causing locking contention between writers
Bitmap indexes must be rebuilt from scratch on every insert
Bitmap indexes only work on tables smaller than memory
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: One update flips bits in two bitmaps, and with compression those bits share segments with many other rows. Engines like Oracle lock whole bitmap segments, so concurrent writers block each other. They aren't rebuilt per insert, and many engines index NULLs in bitmaps.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: PostgreSQL EXPLAIN shows a BitmapAnd over two Bitmap Index Scans followed by a Bitmap Heap Scan. What is happening?
options: PostgreSQL is reading two persistent bitmap indexes created with USING bitmap
Two B-tree indexes are each turned into an in-memory bitmap of matching rows, the bitmaps are AND-ed, and heap pages are visited in physical order
The query is being run twice and the results intersected
The heap is being converted into a column store for the query
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: PostgreSQL has no stored bitmap index type. It builds temporary bitmaps from ordinary indexes, which lets it combine several indexes and read each heap page at most once in physical order.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: Uncompressed, roughly how large is a bitmap index on a country column with 200 distinct values over 1 billion rows?
options: 25 MB
2.5 GB
25 GB
200 GB
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: 200 bitmaps × 1e9 bits = 2e11 bits = 2.5e10 bytes, about 25 GB. Each bitmap is sparse, so run-length or Roaring-style compression shrinks this dramatically in practice. 200 GB forgets to divide bits by 8.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a Bitmap Heap Scan reports 'Heap Blocks: exact=1200 lossy=40000'. What does that indicate?
options: 40,000 heap pages were corrupted and skipped
The bitmap exceeded work_mem and switched to one bit per page, so every row on those pages had to be rechecked
40,000 rows were filtered out by the index condition
The query read 40,000 pages from the OS cache instead of shared buffers
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: When the bitmap can't fit in work_mem, PostgreSQL tracks whole pages instead of individual tuples ('lossy'), and the Recheck Cond must be evaluated on every row of those pages. Raising work_mem for that query can make the scan exact again.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: Which are genuine advantages of bitmap indexes? Select all that apply.
options: AND, OR and NOT across predicates become fast bitwise operations
They are compact for low-cardinality columns, especially when compressed
COUNT(*) for a predicate can be computed by counting set bits
They make concurrent single-row updates cheap
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: Bit operations, compression and popcount-style counting are the strengths. Concurrent single-row updates are the classic weakness, because many rows share each bitmap segment.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: In a data warehouse with bitmap indexes on region, channel and is_returned, which queries benefit most? Select all that apply.
options: WHERE region IN ('EU', 'APAC') AND channel = 'web'
SELECT count(*) WHERE is_returned = true
WHERE order_id = 123456 on a unique column
ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 10
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: Combining low-cardinality predicates (OR within region, AND with channel) and counting matches are the textbook uses. A unique lookup is best served by a B-tree, and top-N by amount needs an ordered index on amount.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: Bitmap indexes are usually a poor fit for unique columns such as a primary key, because each distinct value would need its own almost-empty bitmap.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: With n distinct values you'd have n bitmaps, each with a single set bit. Compression helps, but a B-tree is the natural structure for unique keys.

dbms-storage-indexing:7.prompt: PostgreSQL supports CREATE INDEX ... USING bitmap to create persistent bitmap indexes.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:7.explanation: PostgreSQL's built-in index types are btree, hash, gist, spgist, gin and brin. Its 'bitmap' plans are built at query time from those indexes. Persistent bitmap indexes exist in engines like Oracle.

options: An index on only the first few characters of a text column
An index that only includes rows matching a WHERE predicate given at creation
An index that is only partly loaded into memory
An index on some, but not all, partitions of a table
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: CREATE INDEX ... WHERE predicate indexes only the qualifying rows, so it is smaller and cheaper to maintain. A prefix index (MySQL's col(10)) is a different feature.

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you create CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)). Which query can use it?
options: WHERE email = 'ana@example.com'
WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'
WHERE email ILIKE 'ana@example.com'
WHERE upper(email) = 'ANA@EXAMPLE.COM'
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: An expression index is only used when the query contains the same expression. Plain email, ILIKE and upper(email) are different expressions, so the planner can't match them to lower(email).

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: In PostgreSQL: CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'. Which query can use this index?
options: WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
WHERE status IN ('pending', 'paid') AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
WHERE status <> 'paid' AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: The planner uses a partial index only when it can prove the query's WHERE implies the index predicate. Only status = 'pending' guarantees that; the other queries may need rows the index doesn't contain.

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: A users table uses soft deletes (deleted_at). Emails must be unique among active users only, so a deleted email can be registered again. Which PostgreSQL index enforces this?
options: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email, deleted_at)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
CREATE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: A unique partial index enforces uniqueness only among rows matching its predicate, i.e. active users. (email, deleted_at) doesn't work: NULLs are distinct by default, so two active rows with the same email would both be allowed.

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a query runs as a prepared statement: WHERE status = $1 AND created_at > $2. A partial index exists WHERE status = 'pending'. When a generic plan is used, the index is never chosen, even for $1 = 'pending'. Why?
options: Partial indexes are disabled for prepared statements
Generic plans are made without parameter values, so the planner can't prove the query matches the index predicate
The statistics for partial indexes are only read for literal queries
Prepared statements always use sequential scans
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: Predicate matching happens at plan time. A generic plan has to work for any $1, so it can't assume status = 'pending'. Custom plans (with values known) can use the index, or you can put the literal in the SQL.

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: In PostgreSQL, CREATE INDEX ON events ((created_at::date)) fails when created_at is timestamptz. Why?
options: Expression indexes can't contain casts
date columns can't be indexed with a B-tree
Converting timestamptz to date depends on the TimeZone setting, so the expression isn't IMMUTABLE
The expression needs an extra pair of parentheses
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: Index expressions must give the same result for the same input forever. The calendar date of a timestamptz depends on the session time zone, so the cast is only STABLE. A fixed zone, as in (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date, is immutable.

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: In PostgreSQL you create CREATE INDEX ON docs ((data->>'customerId')) on a jsonb column. Which query can use it?
options: WHERE data @> '{"customerId": "42"}'
WHERE data->>'customerId' = '42'
WHERE data ? 'customerId'
WHERE data->'customerId' = '42'::jsonb
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: A B-tree expression index matches only the exact expression data->>'customerId'. Containment (@>) and key-exists (?) need a GIN index, and data->'customerId' returns jsonb, which is a different expression from ->> (text).

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: What are benefits of a partial index compared with a full index on the same columns? Select all that apply.
options: It is smaller, so more of it stays cached
Rows outside the predicate add no index maintenance on write
It can enforce uniqueness within just a subset of rows
Any query on the indexed columns can use it, whatever its WHERE clause
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: Indexing only the interesting subset cuts size and write cost and allows per-subset uniqueness. A partial index can only be used when the query's WHERE implies the index predicate.

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: In PostgreSQL, given CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)), which queries can use the index? Select all that apply.
options: WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'
WHERE lower(email) IN ('ana@example.com', 'bo@example.com')
WHERE email = 'Ana@Example.com'
WHERE upper(email) = 'ANA@EXAMPLE.COM'
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: Both equality and IN (= ANY) on the same expression match the index. Plain email or upper(email) are different expressions; the planner won't infer that they relate to lower(email).

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: A partial index can only be used by a query whose WHERE clause implies the index's predicate.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: Otherwise the query might need rows the index doesn't contain, and the results would be wrong. PostgreSQL proves the implication at plan time from the query text.

dbms-storage-indexing:8.prompt: In PostgreSQL, an expression index on lower(email) is used automatically for WHERE email ILIKE 'ana@example.com'.
options: True
False
dbms-storage-indexing:8.explanation: ILIKE is a different operator on a different expression, so the planner can't match it to lower(email). Rewrite the query as lower(email) = lower($1), or use the citext type.
